summary: This module covers the fundamentals of Electrical Transformers. It introduces the definition, working principle, and static nature of transformers, explaining why they operate at high efficiencies (96% to 99%) with minimum maintenance. It details the three main components: (i) Primary Winding, (ii) Magnetic Core, and (iii) Secondary Winding, along with the concepts of mutual induction, useful core flux, and leakage flux. The constructional aspects of the laminated silicon steel core are explored, highlighting how laminations reduce eddy current losses and silicon steel reduces hysteresis loss. Furthermore, it presents the comprehensive classification of transformers across six categories: (i) core-type vs. shell-type, (ii) step-up vs. step-down, (iii) purpose (power, distribution, isolation, instrument CT/PT), (iv) windings (two-winding vs. autotransformer), (v) insulation (dry vs. oil-immersed), and (vi) number of phases (single-phase vs. three-phase). Finally, it covers the ideal transformer characteristics (zero resistance, zero leakage, zero iron loss, zero magnetising current) and governing mathematical relations (K = V₂/V₁ = E₂/E₁ = N₂/N₁ = I₁/I₂, E = 4.44 f Φ_m N).

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Define a transformer and explain why it is called a static transformer.
sa.a:
A transformer is an AC machine that:
(i) Transfers electrical energy from one electric circuit to another.
(ii) Does so without a change in frequency.
(iii) Does so by the principle of electromagnetic induction.
(iv) Has electric circuits that are linked by a common magnetic circuit.

It is called a static transformer because it requires no moving parts. Due to this, it has minimum maintenance, no losses due to moving parts (no friction and windage losses), and has maximum efficiency (typical full-load efficiency lies between 96% to 97%; extremely large transformers have efficiencies up to 99%).

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): State the working principle of a transformer and mention the two principles it is based on.
sa.a:
The basic principle behind the working of a transformer is the phenomenon of mutual induction between two windings linked by a common magnetic flux.

The transformer is based on two principles:
(i) An electric current can produce a magnetic field (electromagnetism).
(ii) A changing magnetic field within a coil of wire induces a voltage across the ends of the coil (electromagnetic induction). Changing current in the primary coil changes the magnetic flux that is developed; this changing magnetic flux induces a voltage in the secondary coil.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Differentiate between 'useful flux' (main flux) and 'leakage flux' in a transformer.
sa.a:
(i) Useful Flux (Main Flux): The core provides a magnetic path for the flux to link with the secondary winding. Most of the flux gets linked with both the primary and secondary windings; this is called 'useful flux' or main flux and is responsible for energy transfer.

(ii) Leakage Flux: The magnetic field lines generated due to the primary coil that are not able to link completely with the secondary coil are called 'leakage flux'. Leakage flux links only one winding and gives rise to leakage reactance.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Why is the magnetic core of a transformer laminated and made of silicon steel?
sa.a:
(i) Silicon Steel Material: The material used for core building must be magnetic material with high relative permeability to give a low reluctance path for magnetic flux so it can collect most of the flux produced by primary winding. Silicon steel reduces hysteresis loss.

(ii) Laminated Construction: The magnetic core is made up of thin sheets called laminations of high-grade silicon steel. The laminations break up the path of circulating eddy currents, drastically reducing eddy current losses.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): State the four key assumptions or characteristics of an Ideal Transformer.
sa.a:
An ideal transformer has the following four characteristics:
(i) No winding resistance (R₁ = 0, R₂ = 0; hence zero copper loss I²R = 0).
(ii) No magnetic leakage (100% of flux is confined within the core and links both coils).
(iii) No iron loss (zero hysteresis loss and zero eddy current loss).
(iv) Zero magnetising current (the core has infinite permeability, requiring negligible current to set up flux).

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Differentiate between Step-up and Step-down transformers.
sa.a:
(i) Step-Up Transformer: Secondary voltage is greater than primary voltage (V₂ > V₁, N₂ > N₁). Consequently, secondary current is lower than primary current (I₂ < I₁). Used at generating power stations to raise voltage for transmission.

(ii) Step-Down Transformer: Secondary voltage is lower than primary voltage (V₂ < V₁, N₂ < N₁). Consequently, secondary current is higher than primary current (I₂ > I₁). Used in distribution substations to step down voltage to safe consumer utilization levels.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Compare Core-Type and Shell-Type transformers in terms of construction and flux path.
sa.a:
(i) Core Type Transformer:
- The windings surround/encircle a major part of the magnetic core.
- Has two limbs and a single closed magnetic circuit carrying full flux Φ.
- LV winding is placed inside next to the core, and HV winding is placed outside.

(ii) Shell Type Transformer:
- The magnetic core surrounds/encloses the windings.
- Has three limbs (central limb and two outer limbs). The central limb carries full flux Φ, which divides equally into Φ/2 in each outer limb. Both LV and HV windings are wound on the central limb.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): What is an Autotransformer? State its main advantage and disadvantage compared to a two-winding transformer.
sa.a:
An Autotransformer is a transformer that consists of a single continuous winding wound on a laminated magnetic core, part of which serves as the primary and part (or whole) serves as the secondary.

(i) Advantage: Requires considerably less copper, has smaller size, lower cost, higher efficiency, and superior voltage regulation.
(ii) Disadvantage: Lacks electrical isolation between primary and secondary circuits, so a fault on the high-voltage side directly exposes the low-voltage side to high voltage.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Differentiate between a Power Transformer and a Distribution Transformer.
sa.a:
(i) Power Transformer: Used in transmission substations at generating stations and bulk receiving points. Rated above 200 kVA. Designed for maximum efficiency at or near full rated load (100% load), as it operates continuously loaded.

(ii) Distribution Transformer: Used in local distribution networks to feed residential and commercial consumers. Rated up to 200 kVA. Designed for high 'all-day efficiency' (maximum efficiency at 50% to 70% load) because it operates under widely fluctuating loads 24 hours a day.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): What are Instrument Transformers? Name the two main types.
sa.a:
Instrument Transformers are specialized high-accuracy transformers used to step down high voltages and large currents to safe, standardized levels for measuring instruments (voltmeters, ammeters) and protective relays.

The two types are:
(i) Current Transformer (CT): Steps down high line currents to a standard secondary current (e.g., 5 A) for ammeter measurement.
(ii) Potential Transformer (PT): Steps down high transmission voltages to a standard secondary voltage (e.g., 110 V) for voltmeter measurement.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) With the aid of a neat schematic diagram, explain the construction and working principle of a single-phase transformer. (8 marks)
(b) Explain why a transformer cannot operate on a direct current (DC) supply. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Construction and Working of a Single-Phase Transformer:

1. Major Components:
A transformer has three main components:
(i) Primary Winding: Coupled to an alternating electrical source (V₁); results in the production of alternating magnetic flux.
(ii) Magnetic Core: Made of high relative permeability silicon steel laminations, providing a low-reluctance path for flux linked to secondary winding, forming a closed magnetic circuit.
(iii) Secondary Winding: Links the flux created by primary winding and provides the output voltage (V₂) and current to the load.

2. Working Principle:
- An alternating voltage source V₁ is connected to the primary winding, producing an alternating current i that creates a time-varying magnetic flux Φ in the core.
- The core provides a low-reluctance path, channeling the flux to link with the secondary winding.
- According to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, an alternating EMF E is induced in the secondary side:
  Mutually induced EMF: E₂ = -N₂ (dΦ/dt)  (at the same frequency as supplied EMF).
- If the secondary circuit is closed across a load, mutually induced current I₂ flows through it, transferring electrical energy from primary to secondary.
- The flux in the core also links the primary coil, producing a self-induced EMF E₁ = -N₁ (dΦ/dt) that opposes the applied voltage (back EMF of primary).
- Transformation ratio: K = V₂ / V₁ = E₂ / E₁ = N₂ / N₁ = I₁ / I₂.

(b) Why a Transformer Cannot Operate on a DC Supply:
(i) A transformer functions on Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, which strictly requires a time-varying magnetic flux (dΦ/dt ≠ 0).
(ii) When connected to a DC supply, direct current produces a steady, unchanging magnetic flux (dΦ/dt = 0).
(iii) Consequently, no self-induced back EMF (E₁) is produced in the primary winding to oppose the applied voltage.
(iv) The current is limited only by the extremely low ohmic resistance of the primary winding (I₁ = V / R₁).
(v) A dangerously high current flows, causing rapid overheating and burning out the winding within seconds.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) Classify transformers based on: (i) core construction, (ii) voltage conversion, (iii) purpose, (iv) windings, (v) insulation used, and (vi) number of phases. (8 marks)
(b) Compare Core-Type and Shell-Type transformers with neat sketches showing flux paths. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Classification of Transformers:
Transformers are classified across six major categories:
(i) Types based on transformer's core: Core Type Transformer, Shell Type Transformer.
(ii) Types based on voltage conversion: Step Up Transformer, Step Down Transformer.
(iii) Types based on its purpose: Power Transformer, Distribution Transformer, Isolation Transformer, Current Transformer, Potential Transformer.
(iv) Transformer types based on windings: Two Winding Transformer, Autotransformer.
(v) Transformer types based on insulation used: Dry Type Transformer, Oil Immersed Transformer.
(vi) Transformer types based on number of phases: Single Phase Transformer, Three Phase Transformer.

(b) Comparison of Core-Type and Shell-Type Transformers:
(i) Core Type Transformer:
  • Construction: Windings surround a major part of the magnetic core.
  • Limbs: Has two limbs and two yokes.
  • Magnetic Circuit: Single closed magnetic path carrying full flux Φ.
  • Winding Placement: LV winding is placed next to core on both limbs, and HV winding is placed over LV winding.
  • Dismantling: Simpler to dismantle and repair.
(ii) Shell Type Transformer:
  • Construction: The magnetic core surrounds the windings.
  • Limbs: Has three limbs (central limb and two outer limbs).
  • Magnetic Circuit: Central limb carries full flux Φ, which divides equally into Φ/2 in each outer limb; central limb cross-sectional area is twice that of outer limbs.
  • Winding Placement: Both LV and HV windings are placed in sandwich/interleaved form on the central limb.
  • Mechanical Protection: Better mechanical protection against short-circuit forces.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) Explain the concept of an Ideal Transformer, stating its four fundamental assumptions and transformation ratio relations. (6 marks)
(b) Discuss the various losses occurring in a practical transformer and explain how each loss is minimized. (6 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Ideal Transformer & Transformation Relations:
An ideal transformer is a theoretical machine having 100% efficiency and zero energy losses.

Four Fundamental Assumptions:
(i) No winding resistance: Winding resistances R₁ = 0 and R₂ = 0, so copper loss I²R = 0 and terminal voltages equal induced EMFs (V₁ = E₁, V₂ = E₂).
(ii) No magnetic leakage: 100% of flux is confined within the core and links both coils (no leakage reactance).
(iii) No iron loss: Zero hysteresis loss and zero eddy current loss in the core.
(iv) Zero magnetising current: Magnetic core has infinite permeability, requiring negligible current to set up flux.

Mathematical Relations:
- Induced EMFs: E₁ = 4.44 f Φ_m N₁,  E₂ = 4.44 f Φ_m N₂
- EMF per turn: E₁ / N₁ = E₂ / N₂ = 4.44 f Φ_m
- Transformation Ratio: K = V₂ / V₁ = E₂ / E₁ = N₂ / N₁ = I₁ / I₂.

(b) Losses in a Practical Transformer and Their Minimization:
(i) Core Losses (Iron Losses, P_i):
  • Hysteresis Loss (W_h): Caused by continuous reversal of magnetic domains every AC half-cycle: W_h = η B_max¹·⁶ f V. Minimized by using high-grade silicon steel with a narrow hysteresis loop.
  • Eddy Current Loss (W_e): Caused by circulating eddy currents induced in the core mass: W_e = K_e B_max² f² t² V. Minimized by constructing the core from thin insulated laminations (thickness t = 0.35 mm to 0.5 mm) coated with varnish.
(ii) Copper Losses (Ohmic Losses, P_cu):
  • Caused by electrical resistance of primary and secondary windings: P_cu = I₁² R₁ + I₂² R₂. Minimized by using high-conductivity electrolytic copper conductors with adequate cross-sectional area.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) Explain the constructional details of the transformer core and explain the role of laminations and silicon steel. (6 marks)
(b) A 20 kVA, 2000/200 V, 50 Hz single-phase transformer has 66 turns on the secondary winding. Assuming an ideal transformer, determine: (i) Primary winding turns, (ii) Full-load primary and secondary currents, and (iii) Maximum value of magnetic flux in the core. (6 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Constructional Details of Transformer Core:
(i) Purpose: Provides a continuous, low-reluctance magnetic circuit linking the primary and secondary coils.
(ii) Core Material: Made of thin sheets called laminations of high-grade silicon steel (CRGO steel). Silicon steel reduces hysteresis loss by narrowing the B-H loop, and high permeability collects most of the flux produced by primary winding.
(iii) Laminations: Built up from thin laminations (0.35 mm to 0.5 mm thick) insulated from each other by varnish or lacquer, which drastically reduces eddy current losses.

(b) Numerical Calculation:
Given Data:
- Rated Power S = 20 kVA = 20 × 10³ VA
- Primary Voltage V₁ = 2000 V
- Secondary Voltage V₂ = 200 V
- Frequency f = 50 Hz
- Secondary Turns N₂ = 66 turns

(i) Primary Winding Turns (N₁):
Transformation Ratio: K = V₂ / V₁ = 200 / 2000 = 0.1
N₂ / N₁ = V₂ / V₁ = 0.1
66 / N₁ = 0.1  ⇒  N₁ = 66 / 0.1 = 660 turns. (Ans)

(ii) Full-Load Primary and Secondary Currents:
- Rated Power S = V₁ I₁ = V₂ I₂ = 20,000 VA
- Full-load Primary Current: I₁ = 20,000 / V₁ = 20,000 / 2000 = 10 A. (Ans)
- Full-load Secondary Current: I₂ = 20,000 / V₂ = 20,000 / 200 = 100 A. (Ans)

(iii) Maximum Magnetic Flux in Core (Φ_m):
From EMF equation: E₂ = 4.44 f N₂ Φ_m
For an ideal transformer, E₂ = V₂ = 200 V:
200 = 4.44 × 50 × 66 × Φ_m
200 = 14,652 × Φ_m
Φ_m = 200 / 14,652 = 0.01365 Wb = 13.65 mWb. (Ans)
